passage: In the small town of Sirhind, the evening bus dropped Baljeet near the gurdwara, and she walked home slowly, the admission letter from the Chandigarh college folded in her bag. At dinner, she told them. Her mother put down the roti. "After everything we've done for you? Your father worked double shifts for your school fees. And now you want to leave us?" Baljeet's throat tightened. She loved them. She had seen her father's cracked hands. But she also wanted this. Her younger brother Lokesh looked from one face to another. That night Baljeet lay awake, guilty for wanting to go and angry at being made to feel guilty. Why did loving them mean giving up this?

qa.q: What did Baljeet have folded in her bag?
qa.a: She had the admission letter from the Chandigarh college.

qa.q: What mix of feelings kept Baljeet awake?
qa.a: She felt guilty for wanting to leave her family, and also angry that her love for them was being used to make her choose.

qa.q: What could help Baljeet at this point?
qa.a: She could tell her parents calmly that she loves them and is grateful, and invite them to talk about how to stay close while she studies, instead of treating it as either-or.

qa.q: How might Baljeet's mother be feeling?
qa.a: She may be afraid of losing her daughter and feel their sacrifices are being forgotten, which is why her words come out as guilt.

grounding: It shows a young woman told after all we have done for you, feeling guilt and anger because she loves her family and also wants her own life.

passage: The kitchen in Gothenburg smelled of cinnamon buns when Linnea told her father about the art school in Berlin. Lars stopped stirring his coffee. "After everything we did, driving you to every class, paying for every course? And now you're leaving." His voice cracked on the last word. Linnea stared at the table. She wanted to shout, It's because of you that I can do this! But she also wanted to hug him. Her brother Daniel, sixteen, quietly left the room. Later Linnea sat on the stairs, phone in her hand, the acceptance email still open. She felt like a bad daughter for wanting it, and furious at feeling like one.

qa.q: What city is Linnea's art school in?
qa.a: The art school is in Berlin.

qa.q: What was Linnea feeling on the stairs?
qa.a: She felt guilty, like a bad daughter for wanting to go, and furious at being made to feel that way.

qa.q: What could Linnea say to her father to ease this stage?
qa.a: She could tell him that his support is exactly what made this possible and that leaving is not rejecting him, and ask how they can stay close.

qa.q: How might Daniel be affected by the conversation?
qa.a: He probably felt uncomfortable and sad seeing his father and sister hurting, and left quietly to escape the tension.

grounding: It illustrates a young woman hearing after everything we did, torn between love for her parent and wanting her own path, feeling guilt and anger.

passage:
Leela had been accepted into a master's programme in Hyderabad. She told her mother, Shalini, in the kitchen of their Coimbatore home, while Shalini was rolling chapatis.

Shalini didn't look up. "After all we have done for you. Your father's extra shifts. My gold. And now you'll leave us, just when your father's knees are bad?"

Leela's throat went tight. Guilt came first, fast and heavy: her father's knees, her mother's bare wrists where the bangles used to be. Then, right behind it, anger. She hadn't asked for any of it to be a debt.

"Amma, I love you both. I'm not leaving you. I'm going to study."

"It's the same thing."

"It's not." But her voice wobbled.

Shalini kept rolling. Leela stood there, loving her mother and wanting her own life, feeling that she was being asked to pick one. It didn't seem fair.

qa.q: Where was Leela accepted for her master's programme?
qa.a: In Hyderabad.

qa.q: What two feelings hit Leela when her mother spoke?
qa.a: First guilt, fast and heavy, about her parents' sacrifices, then anger that their help was being treated as a debt.

qa.q: What could Leela do to avoid being forced to choose?
qa.a: Acknowledge her parents' sacrifices, then explain calmly how she can study and still support them, perhaps with a plan for visits and help at home.

qa.q: What might Shalini be feeling as she keeps rolling chapatis?
qa.a: She may be afraid of losing Leela and worried about the family, so the fear comes out as guilt-laden words.

grounding: Leela hears "after all we have done for you" when she chooses to study away, feeling guilt and anger at being forced to choose between her parents and her own life.

"Payal, sit. We need to talk about this Pune job."

"Amma, I've already said yes."

"Without asking us?"

"I'm twenty-two. It's my career."

"After all we have done for you, Payal. We sent you to the best college. Your father took a loan. I stopped working so I could be home for you."

"I know that, Amma."

"Do you? Because it seems you've forgotten."

"I haven't forgotten. I think about it every day."

"Then stay. Find something here."

"There's nothing here in my field."

"So your field is more important than your family."

"That's not fair, Amma."

"Life isn't fair."

"I love you. I want to make you proud. But I can't live my whole life to pay you back."

Sangeeta's eyes filled. Payal's did too. Neither of them looked away.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta give up so she could be home for Payal?
qa.a: She stopped working.

qa.q: What is Payal feeling when she says she can't live her whole life to pay them back?
qa.a: Payal feels torn between love and guilt on one side and anger at the unfairness on the other, forced to choose.

qa.q: What could help both of them at this point?
qa.a: Taking a pause, then talking about what each fears and needs, like how Payal will stay close from Pune, instead of trading sacrifices.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta be feeling when her eyes fill?
qa.a: She is probably hurt and afraid of losing Payal, and perhaps moved by Payal's love.

grounding: In dialogue Payal hears "after all we have done for you" about a job in Pune, and feels guilt, anger and love at being forced to choose between family and her own life.

passage:
The call from my mother came while Bhavna and I were eating momos outside the college gate in Shillong.

I'd told my parents the week before that I wanted to join an NGO in Guwahati after graduation instead of the government exam coaching they'd planned. Mom's voice on the phone was quiet. "After all we have done for you. Your father worked two jobs so you could study. And now you want to throw it away?"

I felt it in my stomach: guilt, heavy and old. Then anger, right behind it. I never asked them to make it a debt.

I said, "Mom, I love you. I'm not throwing anything away." She hung up.

Bhavna put her plate down. "You okay?"

"No. I feel like I'm being asked to choose between them and me. And I love them. That's what makes it so unfair."

She squeezed my hand. We didn't finish the momos.

— Lalremsiami

qa.q: Where does Lalremsiami want to work after graduation?
qa.a: At an NGO in Guwahati.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami feel after Mom's words?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt heavy, old guilt, then anger that the parents' support had been turned into a debt.

qa.q: What could help Lalremsiami at this stage?
qa.a: Talking again when calmer, thanking the parents for their sacrifices, and explaining the plan clearly, so loving them and choosing this path don't feel opposed.

qa.q: How does Bhavna respond to her friend's distress?
qa.a: Bhavna notices, asks if Lalremsiami is okay and squeezes the friend's hand in support.

grounding: Lalremsiami hears "after all we have done for you" about her career choice and feels guilt and anger, loving her parents but wanting her own life.

passage: College counselling notes, Wednesday. Sonali came in today; her friend Yamini waited outside. Sonali has been offered a place in a six-month design residency in Ahmedabad. When she told her parents, her mother said, "After all we have done for you, this is how you repay us?" Sonali repeated that sentence to me three times during the session, each time more quietly. She said, "I love them. I'd do anything for them. And I'm so angry I can't breathe." Then she apologised for being angry. She described feeling that she must pick: be a good daughter or have a life. I told her that guilt and anger can both be true at once, and that loving her parents and choosing her path are not opposites. We practised how she might speak to them. She will come back on Monday, and she has the helpdesk number for the weekend.

qa.q: How long is the design residency in Ahmedabad?
qa.a: It is a six-month residency.

qa.q: What is Sonali feeling when she repeats her mother's sentence three times?
qa.a: She feels guilty and angry at once, loving her parents but furious at being made to choose, even apologising for her anger.

qa.q: What did the counsellor offer that helps at this stage?
qa.a: The counsellor said guilt and anger can both be true, that loving her parents and choosing her path are not opposites, and practised how she might talk to them.

qa.q: What might Sonali's mother be feeling when she says 'After all we have done for you'?
qa.a: Her mother may feel hurt and afraid of losing Sonali, and that fear comes out as a guilt-laden reproach.

grounding: Shows a young adult hearing 'after all we have done for you' and feeling guilt and anger together, loving her parents while wanting her own life.
